To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
A novel reassortant avian influenza A (H10N7) virus was detected in 11 out of 12 seals that died during an epizootic in the Baltic Sea in 2014.
the H10N7 virus was isolated from the respiratory tract of a dead seal and that the seal was positive for H10N7 RNA in lung, nasal, oral, and cloacal swabs.
A novel influenza A (H10N7) virus was isolated from a dead harbour seal in Sweden, which was associated with the mass mortality event in the Baltic Sea in the spring of 2014.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the etiological agent of the mass mortalities that occurred in the Swedish harbour seal ( Phoca vitulin a ) population in the Baltic Sea during March–October 2014.
the investigation of the cause of mass mortality of harbour seal in Sweden during spring and autumn 2014.
the identification and characterisation of the avian influenza (AI) virus that was detected in a large number of harbour seals that died during 2014 in Sweden.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the H 10 N7 virus, which was detected in the lungs of 2 out of 5 seal samples tested in this investigation, is the most likely candidate for the causative agent of the 2014 harbour seal mortality in Sweden.

the mass mortality of harbour seal pups during the 2014 breeding season on the Swedish east coast, was caused by a novel influenza A (H10N7) virus, which was most likely transmitted to seals from gulls.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found a novel avian influenza (AIV) virus (H 10 N 8 ) in a harbour seal ( Phoca vitlulina ) from Sweden in 2014.
the H10N7 virus is a novel reassortant of the Eurasian lineage, with the HA and NA segments originating from North American H10N7 strains and the other segments from Eurasian strains.
we have found a new influenza A virus (IAV) in a new host, harbour seals, which was circulating during a mass mortality of seals in Sweden during spring and autumn 2014.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the 2014 H10N7 virus was a novel reassortant that was able to cause severe disease in seals and was associated with a large die off.
we have found the first evidence of a seal mortality outbreak caused by a novel reassortant avian influenza A virus (AIV).
the H10N7 virus, which is not known to infect seals, caused a mass mortality in a large number of seals.
